extracted.intended_audience: artists, art-critics, students of art and connoisseurs
extracted.subtask_description: Critical/practical guidance for evaluating and producing visual art (painting/sculpture/landscape) emphasizing truth, beauty, relation, power, and qualities of execution. Intended as a general theory for critics and artists to judge merit and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of imitation (definition and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate and present perception that something produced by art is not what it seems to be; the pleasure of imitation is the simple pleasure of surprise produced when one sense is contradicted by another and the mind perceives the thing to be different from its apparent presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation extends only to the sensation of trickery and deception occasioned by a thing's intentionally seeming different from what it is; the degree of pleasure depends on degree of difference and the perfection of the resemblance. Examples: painting and wax-work produce high deceptive pleasure; a chalk outline looks like chalk and paper and thus gives an idea but is not full imitation. Prefer the phrasing 'that it is not what it seems to be' to emphasize the subsequent perception of falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation gives a contemptible pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures derived from imitation are mean and paltry—akin to the surprise of jugglery—and render high or noble emotion physically impossible while the mind exults in sensual surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the spectator must reject the impression of the thing represented and attend to its falsehood, imitation precludes simultaneous high/noble emotion; tears caused by art viewed as deception cannot be the same as tears caused by real agony. Treat deception-derived pleasure as the lowest form of artistic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is limited to contemptible subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that rely on deceptive imitation are either of mean and paltry subjects or show imitation only in contemptible parts (bits of dress, jewels, furniture), because truly great things cannot be imitated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can paint a cat or a fiddle so they look takeable, but you cannot imitate the ocean, the Alps, a tree, or a rainbow. Thus pictures that display deceptive powers are narrow in subject and rank inferior in artistic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is contemptible because it is easy
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceptive imitation requires little more than a true eye, a steady hand, and moderate industry, and so is no higher than neat-handed artificery; it lacks ideas of power and is therefore contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To the instructed, a juggler may be more respectable than an imitative painter because sleight-of-hand implies greater ingenuity; exceptions are the Diorama and the stage where pleasure is of a noble order but still inferior to genuine nature or truthful art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth (definition as applied to art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth in art is the faithful statement, either to the mind or senses, of any fact of nature; we receive an idea of truth when we perceive the faithfulness of such a statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth vs imitation — scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is limited to material things; truth refers both to qualities of material things and to emotions, impressions, and thoughts—there is moral and material truth, with truth of impression/thought far more important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth is a term of universal application; imitation is limited to the narrow field of art dealing with material resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth can be conveyed by non-imitative signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth may be stated by any signs or symbols that have definite signification, even though the signs themselves are no likeness of anything; imitation, by contrast, requires likeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If painting could operate like words—by being taken as a symbol and substitute—it could convey uncorrupted truth without resembling its facts. Truth speaks to the conceptive faculties, imitation to the perceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single attribute can convey truth whereas imitation requires many
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea of truth can exist in the statement of one attribute of anything; an idea of imitation requires the resemblance of as many attributes as are usually cognizant in the object's real presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a pencil outline gives an idea of truth of form without being an imitation; accumulating ideas of truth yields imitation only after several are combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate truths are not necessary for inducing imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: For deception it suffices to approach the simple truths that the senses commonly perceive (distance and projection, coarse truth of form and color); refined truths of color/form may be omitted without losing the power of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The senses are chiefly cognizant of space and projection; coarse resemblances plus careful shading can deceive even with anatomical or form inaccuracies (example: painting an arm with dislocated articulation but with proper broad outlines and shading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of truth are inconsistent with ideas of imitation; truth is foundational
rubrics_metrics.description: When ideas of truth are grouped to give imitation they lose their essence and become corrupted; hence ideas of truth are the foundation of art and imitation its destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude that no picture can be good if it deceives by imitation, because nothing can be beautiful which is not true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Any material object which gives pleasure in the simple contemplation of its outward qualities without direct and definite exertion of the intellect is (in some degree) beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why certain forms/colors please is ultimately instinctive; cultivated taste refines these instincts to derive pleasure from what illustrates moral nature. Beauty here is primarily a moral, not intellectual, perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect taste is the faculty of receiving the greatest possible pleasure from those material sources which are attractive to our moral nature in its purity and perfection; lacking or false taste deviates from this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A man of taste derives maximum pleasure from proper material sources; one who takes pleasure from other sources has false taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between taste and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the instinctive and instant preferring of one material object to another without obvious reason; judgment is a definite intellectual action applicable to many subjects (truth, justice, difficulty, excellence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a perceiver can explain why he likes an object by distinct thought, then the experience moves from taste toward an 'idea of relation' (intellectual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty may involve intellectual perception but remains distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: High ideas of beauty can depend on delicate, untraceable perceptions of fitness and relation (intellectual), but without direct exertion of intellect; if one can articulate reasons, the experience is of relation rather than mere beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Every species of object has an utmost degree of specific beauty—the ideal—which coexists with the object's other perfections; ideas of beauty lead to knowledge of the ideal subjects of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of relation (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of relation comprise all those conveyed by art that are subjects of distinct intellectual perception and action—expression, sentiment, character, the conception of the subject and congruity/relation of its parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ideas are expressed by particular choices (e.g., a choice of incident or light) that give expression and meaning beyond technical workmanship; they can often be conveyed equally by words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of relation (nobility and primacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of relation are the noblest sources of pleasure in art, superior to mere beauty or execution; they give expression and meaning and thus subordinate other sources of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work conveying strong ideas of relation (expression, character) is of higher rank even if its outward form is less ideally beautiful; examples: Turner's choice of incident vs Claude's decorative detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of power — general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of power arise from the accuracy, certainty, and rapidity with which difficulty is vanquished and knowledge is expressed; power is felt both as an estimate of unseen difficulty and as a sensation when seen in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power often accompanies other high ideas (truth, beauty, relation) and cannot be wholly separated from them. Beware of preferring mere sensation of power to the intellectual estimate of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of receiving ideas of power
rubrics_metrics.description: One mode is by perfect knowledge of difficulty and means (estimate); the other is by sensation when power is visibly in operation (sensation). If both agree and sensation equals estimate, one receives the utmost idea of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works often present inconsistent estimate and sensation; only rarely (e.g., Michelangelo) do both align fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation of power stronger in unfinished works but should not be preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Half-completed or rapidly executed works often give a greater sensation of power (because action is seen and means seem inadequate), yet the true superiority lies in the completed work that attains the perfect end with the slightest possible means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the highest estimate of power (completion with no wasted touch) over the keenest mere sensation from incompleteness; greatest power is in works where 'all has been done, and yet not a touch thrown away.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Execution is the right mechanical use of the means of art to produce a given end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary quality of execution: truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The first quality of execution is a delicate and ceaseless expression of refined truth carried out to the last touch; this 'truth of truths' is the distinguishing merit that even surpasses other technical qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowest draughtsmen can match swiftness or simplicity but not the precision of truth; if truth of manipulation is present, other qualities may be spared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution quality: simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity is the second quality: unpretending, quiet, retiring means are more impressive; ostentation, brilliancy, or making lines attractive at the expense of meaning is vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution quality: mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery (third quality) — nature is mysterious in her means; art that is most inexplicable and defies imitation is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Execution that is incomprehensible and therefore hard to imitate (other things equal) is superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution quality: inadequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Inadequacy (fourth quality) — the less sufficient the means appear relative to the end, the greater the sensation of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contributes to the feeling of power but must be balanced against truth and completeness; it is one legitimate source of pleasure in execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution quality: decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision (fifth quality) — the appearance that whatever is done has been done fearlessly and at once; this indicates perfect knowledge of the fact and the means necessary to represent it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision gives impression of knowledge and should accompany execution where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution quality: velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocity (sixth quality) — quickness of touch is agreeable because it suggests decision and power; of two otherwise equal touches the quickest is generally best, giving lines more evenness, grace, and natural qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick touches better resemble natural lines—gradation, uncertainty, and unity—and are preferable when truth is equally present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strangeness as an illegitimate/conditional source of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Strangeness (possible seventh quality) can produce pleasure when other higher qualities are secured, by using means unexpected or unthought-of, but it is scarcely a right or primary source of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combined with truth and other virtues, novel means can enhance impression (example: Rubens' surprising ground and few bold touches), but strangeness alone is not a legitimate substitute for fundamental qualities.
